standard_prerequisites.name: Mere proposition
standard_prerequisites.statement: A proof of is-prop(A) assigns to every pair of points a path between them.

standard_prerequisites.name: Dependent action on paths
standard_prerequisites.statement: For a dependent function g the action on paths of g at p is a dependent path between the transports of its values.
standard_prerequisites.use: It is the step that produces the equation for an arbitrary path.

standard_prerequisites.name: Transport in a path family computes by concatenation
standard_prerequisites.statement: Transporting a path in the family of paths out of a point computes as concatenation, so the dependent path becomes an explicit concatenation identity.
standard_prerequisites.use: It turns the dependent path into the equation that kills both paths.

core_obligations: Fix a proof f of propositionality and a point x, and define the function sending y to the path f(x,y) (source lines 325-326).
Apply the dependent action on paths of that function to an arbitrary path p from y to z (source lines 326-327).
Use the computation of transport in the path family to turn that dependent path into the equation that p equals the inverse of one value concatenated with the other (source lines 327-328).
Conclude that any two paths between x and itself are equal, since both are given by the same expression (source lines 328-330).

proof_roadmap.step: Fix the propositionality proof and define the auxiliary function.
Apply the dependent action on paths and compute the transport.
Conclude that all loops at a point coincide.

difficulty_reason: Counted unit is the author labelled lemma at source lines 321-323 (book Lemma 3.3.4): every mere proposition is a set. The statement is a level implication and the proof (source lines 324-330) has to exhibit the uniformity of paths rather than merely assert it: it fixes a point and turns the propositionality proof into a function into the path family, applies the dependent action on paths of that function to an arbitrary path, computes the resulting dependent path through the transport rule in a path family to obtain an explicit equation expressing that path by two values of the auxiliary function, and then observes that any two loops at the point are given by the same expression. The transport computation is the core and it is not visible in the statement.
